--- ABSTRACT ---
[AIMS]: To determine the efficacy of screening women under age 50 with a significant family history of breast cancer.
[METHODS]: Results from 22 Breast Units in the UK identified as being able to provide data were surveyed and pooled through regional data managers or consultant breast specialists.
[RESULTS]: Data relating to 8783 women screened and 9075 woman years of follow-up was analysed. Cancer incidence was 11.3/1000/year. The rate of cancer detection was 4. 78/1000 at prevalent screening and 4.52/1000 at incident screening. Median age at diagnosis was 43 years. Interval cancers presented at a rate of 2.45/1000. Comparison with the National Health Service Breast Screening Programme for women aged 50-64 revealed a similar rate of cancer detection and a similar incidence of ductal carcinoma in situ. The pathological features of screen-detected cancers in this study strongly suggest that prognosis for these women is more favourable than if they had presented symptomatically.
[CONCLUSIONS]: This study provides evidence to suggest that screening young women with a significant family history of breast cancer is effective and that a survival benefit can be expected. As a result the British Familial Breast Cancer Group proposes a co-ordinated prospective observational study.

[BACKGROUND]: Evidence supports a reduction in mortality from breast cancer with mammographic screening in the general population of women aged 40-49 years, but the effect of family history is not clear. [INTERPRETATION]: Yearly mammography in women with a medium familial risk of breast cancer is likely to be effective in prevention of deaths from breast cancer.

The abstract reports that screen-detected tumors had more favorable pathological features and concludes screening was effective with an expected survival benefit, but it does not provide observed mortality or a randomized mortality comparison.

source_tools.relevance: Exact publication identification and abstract results

key_findings.finding: The direct prospective UK follow-up study was FH01: 'Mammographic surveillance in women younger than 50 years who have a family history of breast cancer: tumour characteristics and projected effect on mortality...' (Lancet Oncology, 2010), PMID 21093374. It enrolled 6,710 women at intermediate familial risk from 76 UK centres, with annual mammography; mean follow-up was 4 years (SD 2). Among 136 cancers, 105 (77%) were screen-detected, 28 (21%) interval symptomatic cancers, and 3 (2%) occurred after nonattendance. Invasive cancers were significantly smaller, less node-positive, and more favorable grade than UK Age Trial controls; node positivity was also lower than in a Dutch familial-history comparison. Projected 10-year mortality was 1.10% versus 1.38% in UK Age Trial controls, adjusted relative risk 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.96; p=0.022). The authors concluded annual mammography was likely to prevent breast-cancer deaths, but this was a single-arm observational study using projected—not observed—mortality.

source_tools.relevance: Exact population, follow-up, cancer detection, tumor characteristics, and projected mortality

key_findings.finding: The full FH01 cohort evaluation (HTA 2013), PMID 23489892, included 6,710 women recruited 2003–2007 from 74 UK centres, generally aged 40–49 with at least a 3% breast-cancer risk during ages 40–49, offered annual mammography for at least 5 years. By December 2010 there were 165 cancers over 37,025 person-years and 30,556 screening episodes; 122 (74%) were screen-detected and 44 (27%) were DCIS. The model estimated 19 breast-cancer deaths (6.3/1,000/year) versus 204 predicted deaths in 622,127 person-years in UK Age Trial controls (2.4/1,000/year), yielding an estimated 40% mortality reduction (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37–0.98; p=0.04). The report concluded annual mammography was clinically effective and cost-effective, while acknowledging the need for further research. This remains modeled evidence from a single-arm cohort, not direct mortality evidence.

source_tools.relevance: Expanded cohort size, observation time, detection, DCIS, and mortality estimate

key_findings.finding: Overall interpretation: these UK studies support offering annual mammographic surveillance to carefully risk-defined women under 50 with significant/moderate familial risk, because cancers were frequently screen-detected and had more favorable prognostic features, with consistently favorable projected mortality estimates. However, they do not establish benefit through a randomized trial or observed mortality endpoint; conclusions are vulnerable to lead-time, length-time, selection, and comparison-group/modeling biases. A DOI was not available in the retrieved PubMed abstracts/content, so it should not be inferred without a bibliographic lookup.
